The Financial Analyst Memo: every financial table and model output behind this memo

OEM International (OEM.B-SE): a very good compounder with steady earnings and a volatile share price, whose risk/reward turns unusually positive only after a capital framework or a 2027 mark-down

10 November 2026. Share price SEK 171.0 (29 October 2026, the latest price in the files). Money in SEK millions unless stated; per-share figures in SEK. Notes on the forecast basis and the sources are in the end notes.

Summary

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

The business. OEM is a very good Swedish technical trader: it acts as the outsourced local sales arm for more than 400 component makers, earns returns on capital above 30%, held its margin through three downturns and has net cash. In February 2025 EQT took control and turned a company that accumulated cash into one that buys six to eight small companies a year out of its own cash flow. That change has already happened; it is not a promise.

The case in one line. OEM is a low-variance earnings case inside a high-variance share-price case. OEM's 2027 earnings should land within about 8% of the model either way; OEM's share price will be set by the multiple of the whole Swedish compounder group and by three company events in the next six months.

Earnings: low varianceset by OEM’s own delivery; the 2027 EPS range is in #9
Share price: high varianceset by the group multiple and by three company events in six months; the 18-month return cases are in #12

The crux of the case is the sequence of earnings revisions, not the valuation.

2026 · the exceptional year

2026 is an exceptional year, lifted by the cycle and a weaker krona, and its results are nearly banked.

2027 · the digestion year

2027 is a digestion year. Tough comparisons, the end of one large Irish project, a small margin give-back, higher central costs and the absence of 2026’s one-off financial gains all land in the same year. Model EPS grows about 4%, below every broker on a like-for-like basis.

2028 onward · the compounder

From 2028 OEM settles into about 5% organic growth plus 6% acquired growth, and EPS grows about 12% a year without leverage. The model is above consensus here, because consensus counts only signed deals.

▲ up to April 2027▼ July and October 2027▲ up again, for a different reason

The likely path of OEM’s earnings estimates is therefore up to April 2027, down in July and October 2027, and up again afterwards for a different reason: new deals and, probably, a capital framework.

Four insights Richard should not miss.

1
Upside not in the numbers

OEM’s unused balance sheet is a free, probable and undated option. Without leverage, OEM’s return on equity slides below the company’s own 25% target by 2027. EQT has set a leverage range at every listed company it has controlled. I put the odds of a capital framework at about even by the February 2028 results. A framework is worth about 15% on EPS and is in no broker’s numbers.

2
Resilience the market does not weight

A de-rating cannot stop OEM’s acquisition engine. OEM pays for its deals in cash from free cash flow. The roll-ups that failed (Storskogen, and Bufab in 2022) were stopped by their funding. The market mentions this resilience in passing and does not weight it.

3
Dependence

The 18-month return depends on deals not yet signed, under a chief executive not yet named. Without the unsigned deals, the 18-month return at the working fair multiple falls to about zero (arithmetic in #9).

4
Quality of the 2026 margin

OEM’s 2026 margin gain came through the gross margin (currency and mix), not through operating leverage. The new central organisation absorbed the fixed-cost leverage that 16% sales growth should have produced. Brokers still forecast margin expansion in 2027; the model has a small dip.

Skew todayNot unusual yettiming, not value

Richard's test: is the risk/reward skew unusually positive? Not today, and the reason is timing. Fundamental outcomes skew up over 18 to 36 months, because brokers do not model the acquisition engine, the leverage option is free and free cash flow is about to inflect. Estimate revisions skew down from mid-2027. Valuation gives no help: the stock trades at the group multiple, and the model’s return is roughly the business’s own compounding rate less a one-off de-rating. The skew becomes unusually positive if either of two things happens: OEM announces a capital framework, or the market marks the multiple down during the second-half 2027 slowdown while the acquisition engine keeps running. Both triggers can be dated, so OEM is a case to track closely, not one to file.

Five judgements move the shares (each is sized in #9): the organic growth rate in the second half of 2027; whether the gross margin holds near 37%; whether the deal cadence survives the change of chief executive; whether and when the owner uses the balance sheet; and the multiple on which the Swedish compounder group trades.

The dated tests.
  1. 31 Dec 2026Successor named
  2. 18 Feb 2027Results: operating cash flow of at least SEK 250m, and the dividend
  3. Spring 2027Annual general meeting: first window for new targets
  4. c.14 Oct 2027Third-quarter 2027 report: the stall test

The operating environment

#1 Tailwinds in the operating environment, and headwinds

Evidence. Demand for OEM’s products has swung up hard and broadly.

5% → 8% → 14%organic growth in the first, second and third quarters of 2026
+40%third-quarter orders; the order backlog rose 57%, to a little under one quarter’s sales
11% or moreorganic growth in every region
60.5Swedish manufacturing PMI in October (euro area 52.7), strengthening again

Peers’ third-quarter reports confirm a broad Nordic upswing. A weaker krona is lifting OEM’s sales and, for a quarter or two, its gross margin.

Three facts qualify the strength of demand.

  • Part of the surge is distributor pre-buying, not end-demand. 42% of distributors in Morgan Stanley’s survey are pre-buying (29% a quarter earlier), while their customers’ behaviour is flat.
  • One large project will not repeat. An Irish data-centre order of about SEK 117m is delivered mainly in the second half of 2026.
  • Construction, about 18% of sales, is still contracting.

The force that sets OEM’s multiple runs the other way: United States ten-year yields near 5.1%, European rate rises priced for 2027, oil above USD 100 and a risk-off market.

Inference. This is OEM’s best operating environment in more than three years. It is mostly cyclical, and its rate of improvement peaks around the fourth quarter of 2026. The durable layer of demand (automation, about half of sales; electrification, grids, data centres and defence) supports organic growth of 5% to 6% a year, not 14%.

The model’s 1% to 2% organic growth for the second half of 2027 is not a bearish call on demand. It is the through-cycle rate of about 5% less up to 3.5 points from the Irish order not repeating, because that order is about 3.5% of second-half 2026 sales. The headline will look like a cycle turning; the substance is one project not repeating.

Why the second half of 2027 looks weak: one project not repeating, not a demand collapse
about 5%underlying organic growth, the through-cycle rate

up to 3.5 ptsthe Irish data-centre order (c.SEK 117m, 3.5% of H2 2026 sales) not repeating

1% to 2%the model’s H2 2027 organic growth: the headline that will look like a turn

So what. Demand supports OEM’s next two quarterly reports well. After them, OEM’s growth rate falls by arithmetic while its level of activity can keep rising: the European upcycle is about six quarters old, against an average length of about fourteen. For a stock on about 25 times earnings, a problem of optics is still a problem for the share price.

Counter-case. Upward: a PMI of 60 and a young cycle argue for a longer upswing, and data-centre and defence projects may repeat (Finland’s data-centre pipeline, Baltic defence spending). In that case the brokers’ 6% organic growth for 2027 is right. Downward: a restock led by distributors while end-customers are flat is the configuration in which order books turn fastest. After past restocking peaks, growth forecasts were wrong by 5 to 15 points within four to six quarters, and earlier rounds of this analysis put the probability of a sharp industrial relapse within 18 months at 15% to 20%.

What would change my view. Up: orders still growing year on year in the second quarter of 2027 against a +23% comparison, or a second large project order in the Rest of Europe segment. Down: Swedish orders falling year on year, or a strengthening krona.

Against the market. Brokers agree with the model on the direction of 2027 but not on its depth: they carry about 6% organic growth for the year, against the model’s 4.6%. I agree with the model for the full year, and would lean the first half higher while keeping the second half as modelled. On the discount rate I agree with the market: the risk is widely discussed and belongs to the whole compounder group, not to OEM alone.

Conclusion: The tailwinds are strong, broad and mostly cyclical, and their rate of improvement peaks around the turn of the year; the one serious headwind, the discount rate, acts on OEM’s multiple rather than on its earnings.

Score: 66, set by the Rater. A broad Nordic upswing (organic growth 5%, 8%, 14% through 2026, orders +40%, every region +11% or more, PMI 60.5) sits on a durable automation, electrification, grid, data-centre and defence layer worth 5-6% organic a year, but it is mostly cyclical, partly distributor pre-buying, peaks in rate around the turn of the year and the Irish project does not repeat, while construction (18% of sales) still contracts; the discount rate acts on the multiple and is scored in topic 9. A clear but fading net positive, slightly above the External change forces group (64) for the structural layer, stronger and broader than Instalco's Nordic recovery but less structural than Eckert & Ziegler's.

Corporate change

#2 Internally driven corporate change, and its problems

Evidence. Almost everything above OEM’s subsidiaries has changed in 20 months.

  • Owner and board. EQT holds 26% of the capital and 74% of the votes, bought at SEK 110 a share. Six of the seven directors were new in 2025. The chair left after 18 months to become chief executive of Straumann, a career move rather than a verdict on OEM, and Patrik Andersson replaced him on 23 October 2026.
  • Executives. OEM appointed a Deputy CEO for strategy and acquisitions in April 2026 and, in August 2026, a CFO who raised Coor’s cash conversion from 57% to 99%. The chief executive of 26 years must leave the role by 31 December 2026, and no file up to 9 November names a successor.
  • Actions. The pace of acquisitions has stepped up from a previous norm of one to three deals a year (figures below). Earn-outs were revalued upward in the third quarter, which means the acquired companies are performing ahead of plan. About SEK 355m of capital spending in 2026, mostly on property and logistics, ends with the Jönköping warehouse in February 2027.
  • Not changed. Formal targets, guidance, shareholder returns and the decentralised operating model are all unchanged.
  • Weaker. Operating cash flow fell while EBITA rose (figures below); group function costs swung by SEK 14m in the third quarter; executives’ variable pay is now up to 200% of salary on one-year measures, with no clawback and no internal audit function.
7deals in twelve months (previous norm: one to three a year)
c.SEK 500mannual sales added, about 9% of the base
c.0.95xsales paid; earn-outs revalued upward (ahead of plan)
−23% vs +24%operating cash flow against EBITA, nine months 2026

Inference. The durable part of the case is here, and it is real. An owner with the votes and the incentive has changed the people, the mandate and the actions of a business whose strengths (high returns, shared logistics that absorb acquired product lines, a model that keeps founders in place, net cash) are the ones such a change needs. The change is still incomplete in the two places that matter most: who runs OEM, and what capital structure the owner wants.

The capital-structure gap is closer to being filled than the market assumes. On the model’s numbers, OEM’s reported return on equity falls from 24.7% to about 22% in 2027 and about 20% by 2029, because profits pile up in an ungeared balance sheet. A target that is missed by arithmetic invites a new target, and EQT set an explicit leverage range at Munters, Beijer Ref and Sanitec. My odds for a new framework are shown below. They are slightly later than those of an earlier round of this analysis, because a new chief executive usually takes two to four quarters before presenting a strategy update.

A framework is worth about 15% on EPS (sized in #9) and is in no broker’s numbers.

So what. The base case needs only that OEM keeps acquiring at about 80% of its 2026 pace under a new leader. The upside case needs a decision that the owner has every reason to take.

Counter-case. The succession could go wrong. The likeliest candidate, the Deputy CEO, is a transaction executive with no operating record at OEM, while OEM’s culture lives in about 35 subsidiary heads and five division heads, several with three decades at the company. Bergman & Beving is the precedent for a centralising reset that cost years of organic growth. EQT’s own record includes Munters, where a new chief executive spent the first phase on internal optimisation rather than deals. And an acquisition organisation is a fixed cost that needs deal flow, which is how discipline on price erodes.

What would change my view. Down: departures of division or subsidiary heads (none disclosed so far); the gap between segment EBITA and group EBITA widening beyond about SEK 15m a quarter; a deal above 10x EBITA. Up: an internal or operationally credible appointment; deals continuing through the first half of 2027; new targets at the annual general meeting.

Against the market. The market treats leverage as an option that may arrive one day; I treat it as a probable event with a mechanical trigger and a time window. The market carries the succession as a general risk. The precedents (Addtech 2018, Indutrade 2017, Lifco 2019, and Beijer Ref in 2021 and again this month with an internal successor) show planned changes at decentralised compounders passing without disruption, so I carry the succession as a 25% to 30% risk of two to four slow quarters, not as the central case. I agree with the market that the step-up in acquisitions is the main story.

Conclusion: OEM’s corporate change is strong, funded and already acting; its most powerful part, the use of the balance sheet, is still to come; and its one open risk is a dated binary event, the appointment of the next chief executive.

Score: 70, set by the Rater. EQT's control has turned a cash accumulator into a self-funded serial acquirer (seven deals in twelve months adding about 9% of sales at about 0.95x sales, earn-outs revalued up, so it is working), with a new board, deputy CEO and cash-focused CFO and a probable leverage framework still to come, which is a large strategic move adding about half of EPS growth from 2028. Net of the internal problems (operating cash flow -23% while EBITA +24%, a central cost build that absorbed 2026's operating leverage, one-year pay with no clawback, and a chief executive leaving without a named successor), I sit above the group's 64 because the change is funded and in the numbers, close to Theon's deliberate pivot and above Redcare's still-unproven one.

Industry and business model

#3 Value chain, industry structure, business model, financial profile and management

Evidence.

  • Industry: fragmented and rational. The top five European technical traders hold under 15% of the market; OEM has about 2% to 3% of a Northern European market worth about EUR 22bn. Competitors are margin-first compounders and small family firms, and there was no price war in the 2023 to 2025 downturn (OEM’s margin record is in the box below).
  • Position in the value chain. OEM is the channel for small foreign manufacturers that cannot afford their own Nordic sales and logistics. OEM avoids carrying competing product lines, which keeps those manufacturers loyal, and no single supplier or customer is large.
  • Advantages. Design-in and technical selling, pooled warehouses with next-day delivery, and long-tenured local managers. These advantages show in share gains (OEM grew organically through a period that included eleven flat quarters at Addtech) and in high returns on capital.
  • Limits. OEM has no demonstrated real pricing power: 70% to 80% of sales is trading in standard products, where the largest accounts extract a price concession every year. The gross margin is about 37%; the 53% to 55% quoted in some older sources is a data error. Working capital is heavy, so growth consumes cash.
  • Management. The outgoing chief executive’s record is excellent (return on invested capital raised from 10% to 28%; a ten-year shareholder return of about 800%) and conservative on capital. Formal goals are unchanged and not stretching. Governance now serves a sponsor: votes are concentrated, the audit committee is not independent of EQT, and directors own almost no shares.
OEM’s moats protect market share and returns, not price

What the structure protects

  • Share: organic growth of 7% a year in 2021 to 2025
  • Returns: 30.7% return on capital employed in 2025
  • Margin in downturns: EBITA 15.0% to 15.8% while organic growth ran −1% to +3%
  • Loyalty: no supplier above 3% of sales, no customer above 4%

What it does not

  • Price: pass-through only; largest accounts extract about 3% a year
  • Gross margin of about 37%, not 53% to 55%
  • Cash in growth: working capital about 25% of sales, 92 days against 65 to 78 at peers
  • Governance: serves a sponsor; top job unfilled from January

Inference. OEM’s industry structure is favourable for a consolidator and ordinary for a price-setter: the moats protect share and returns, not price. OEM’s financial profile is well above average on returns and resilience and below average on cash conversion in growth years. Management quality is proven at the subsidiary layer and unknown at the top from January 2027.

So what. The structure supports the three things the forecasts need: a stable gross margin, modest share gains and a long runway of acquisition targets (about 24,000 candidate companies in Europe, and 10 to 25 proposals a week). The structure does not support margin convergence with product-owning peers such as Lagercrantz or Lifco, and the model does not ask for that convergence.

Counter-case. The structure has two weak points; both act slowly, and both are real. First, entry prices for acquisitions are drifting up as private equity platforms and the listed compounders chase the same targets, and OEM has widened its mandate into the product-owning niches where those peers hunt. Second, price transparency (global digital catalogues, procurement portals) bears on the standard products that make up most of OEM’s sales. Neither weak point should break the model within four years; both lower the return on each new krona invested.

What would change my view. A disclosed deal multiple above 8x to 10x EBITA, acquired companies’ margins below 12%, or a falling gross margin with a stable krona would show that the structure protects OEM less than I think.

Against the market. DNB Carnegie argues that OEM’s “premium quality metrics” justify a proven-compounder multiple. I agree on the returns and the resilience, and differ on two points. First, OEM’s quality is that of a very good distributor rather than a fortress: it has no pricing power and heavy working capital. Second, the sector’s own rule is that cash conversion is the honest scorecard for inventory-heavy distributors, and on that scorecard 2026 is a warning that the market treats as a footnote. The footnote reading is probably right, since OEM’s working-capital build reversed within a year in both 2020 and 2023, but it is unproven for project receivables.

Conclusion: OEM’s industry and business model are favourable and robust for a disciplined consolidator, with high returns and narrow moats; the weak points are cash conversion in growth years, governance under a sponsor and an unnamed chief executive.

Score: 67, set by the Rater. A fragmented, rational industry with no price war in the 2023-25 downturn, no supplier above 3% or customer above 4%, design-in and logistics moats that protect share rather than price, and a margin held at 15.0-15.8% through three downturns; ROIC 22.8% (92nd percentile) and ROE 84th percentile are honest, but new capital earns less (deals at about 14% EBITA margins on 0.95x sales plus working capital at 25% of sales), there is no real pricing power, and governance now serves a sponsor with the top job unfilled. Coherent with the four groups (60, 58, 72, 63), it sits well above Indutrade on returns and predictability but below Volex's certification switching costs, alongside Linea Directa's high-return, narrow-moat profile.

Guidance and delivery

#4 Conservatism of guidance, management of expectations, and the record of delivery

Evidence. OEM gives no numerical guidance. It publishes four through-the-cycle floors (shown below against the model’s 2027), last raised in February 2023 after years of being beaten. The outlook sentence in OEM’s reports barely changes from quarter to quarter, and OEM has never held a capital-markets day. Against consensus EBITA the last four quarters read −8%, +13%, +9% and +4% (chart below); over three years the record is balanced, including a 16% miss in the second quarter of 2025 on a stronger krona. Estimates have risen for twelve months without any steer from the company.

The four floors against the model’s 2027, the new leader’s first year
Floor (set Feb 2023)Model 2027Status
Sales growth at least 10%+9.6%missed by a hair
EBITA margin at least 12%15.8%beaten
Return on equity at least 25%c.22%missed by c.3 pts
Debt to equity below 100%net cashmet
EBITA against consensus over the last four quarters: three beats and one miss, a cyclical rather than a biased record

Inference. OEM’s guidance is conservative in form and useless in function. The floors sit far below delivery on margin, at the edge of delivery on growth and above delivery on return on equity. Nobody at the company manages the bar: three or four brokers set it, and they have raised it steadily. The record is cyclical rather than biased: OEM beats in upswings and misses in downswings and currency shocks, because the brokers lag the cycle in both directions.

So what. Two of Richard’s preferred conditions are absent: there is no sandbagged guidance waiting to be raised, and no management team keeping the sell-side low. What stands in for a guidance raise is the replacement of the floors with a real capital framework (#2). On the model, 2027, the new leader’s first year, misses two of the four floors: sales growth by a hair and return on equity by about three points. Missing the floors is uncomfortable, and it is also the pressure that produces new targets.

Counter-case. A plain reading of the same facts is that OEM under-promises and over-delivers, and always has: its margin has averaged more than three points above the floor, and the 2026 beats were large. If the cycle extends, the brokers’ lag keeps producing beats through 2027.

What would change my view. A capital-markets day, explicit targets, or a CFO-led move to guide on cash and capital would turn OEM’s guidance from uninformative into a source of positive surprise. The new CFO ran investor relations at Coor, which is the best reason to expect such a move.

Against the market. The market reads OEM’s absence of guidance as modesty. I read it as an unmanaged bar that the cycle has already lifted. The market and I agree that the company’s record of acting (in every downturn since 2001, and on deals in 2026) deserves weight.

Conclusion: OEM’s guidance is too thin to be conservative in any useful sense, its record of delivery is strong but cyclical, and the realistic source of a “raise” is a new capital framework rather than a beaten forecast.

Score: 54, set by the Rater. No numerical guidance (not a negative), four floors raised in 2023 of which the margin floor is beaten by three points but the 10% growth floor was missed in 2023-25 and the 25% ROE target is missed now and on the model in 2027; against consensus EBITA the last four quarters read -8%, +13%, +9%, +4%, with a 16% miss in Q2 2025, and estimates have risen for twelve months without any steer. A cyclical rather than biased record with nobody managing the bar puts it about the middle, slightly above the Guidance (47) and Sell-side (46) groups because the recent beats and the margin floor record are real, between Renew's honest-but-cut record and Entra's small-variance tracker.

Levers and loops

#5 Pricing power, operating leverage, financial leverage, cost scope and feedback loops

Evidence and inference, lever by lever.

  • Pricing power: pass-through only. OEM’s contracts carry no inflation clauses; currency clauses cover 68% of sales. OEM recovers cost and currency moves in one to two quarters and loses margin while it waits (the third quarter of 2022 and the second quarter of 2025 are the precedents). Price adds about 2 to 2.5 points to nominal growth in 2027 and nothing to margin.
  • Operating leverage: moderate, and absent in 2026. The contribution margin on organic sales is 25% to 30%, yet in 2026 EBITA is growing only about 1.5 times as fast as sales, against 2.5 times in the 2021 recovery. Cost of goods fell as a share of sales while staff costs rose as a share of sales (figures below), so the whole 2026 margin gain came through the gross margin.
  • Cost-out: a defence, not an upside. OEM has no cost programme and needs none. In a downturn OEM could cut about SEK 40m to 60m of costs within a year and SEK 120m to 180m over two to three years, which would keep the EBITA margin near 14%. Owned warehouses and a central acquisition team make the cost base a little stickier than it was in 2009.
  • Financial leverage: none in use, and a large amount in reserve (sized in #9).
  • Feedback loops: four matter, and the figure below traces each one. The reinvestment flywheel compounds without any equity or debt market in the loop. The working-capital loop stabilises: growth absorbs cash and a slowdown releases it, so OEM’s cash flow moves inversely to its earnings and steadies the balance sheet in a bad year. The amortisation loop hides the acquisition engine: OEM writes off acquired intangibles over four to five years, against ten years at Addtech and Lifco, so on the reported basis a deal earns almost nothing until its sixth year. The return-on-equity loop pushes the owner toward leverage.
1.5x vs 2.5xEBITA growth as a multiple of sales growth: 2026 against the 2021 recovery
62.8% vs c.64%cost of goods as a share of sales: nine months 2026 against 2024. The whole gain came through the gross line
staff costs ↑as a share of sales: the central build spent the operating leverage
OEM’s 2026 margin gain came through the gross margin (currency and mix), not through operating leverage.

So what. In the base case, OEM’s revenue growth does not produce outsized profit growth. From 2028 revenue grows about 11% a year, EBITA about 12.5% and EPS about 12%. The outsized element is entirely in the unused balance sheet: OEM is a steady compounder with an option attached, not a geared recovery story.

The amortisation loop decides which brokers “see” the acquisition engine. Adjusted EPS shows the engine; reported EPS hides it for five years. If OEM moved to ten-year amortisation lives, reported EPS in 2030 would be about SEK 0.55 higher with no change in cash. That change is an easy win for a CFO with an investor-relations background.

Counter-case. Operating leverage could arrive later rather than not at all. Once the central build stops growing faster than sales (in 2028 on the model), each point of organic growth should drop through to EBITA at about 27%, so a cycle that extends into 2028 would show the operating leverage that 2026 did not. Product mix is a second slow lever: modified and proprietary products are 20% to 30% of sales, and the product-owning acquisitions raise that share.

What would change my view. Staff costs falling below 15% of sales with organic growth above 8% would show that operating leverage has arrived. Cost of goods above 63.5% of sales with a stable krona would show that the gross-margin gain is being given back.

Against the market. Brokers expect margin expansion in 2027 (an EBITA margin of 16.2% at DNB Carnegie and 16.3% at Redeye) and medium-term EBITA growth of about 15% a year. The model has a 2027 EBITA margin of about 15.8%, and I agree with the model: the evidence of 2026 is that operating leverage was earned and then spent. On the cash-funded acquisition flywheel I am more positive than the market, which mentions it and does not weight it.

Conclusion: OEM’s business model converts growth into proportionate rather than outsized profit growth, protects the margin well in a downturn, and holds its one true amplifier, financial leverage, in reserve.

Score: 42, set by the Rater. Pricing is pass-through only with a one-to-two-quarter lag, the contribution margin on organic sales of 25-30% against a 16% EBITA margin gives only moderate operating gearing that the central build spent in 2026 (EBITA 1.5x sales growth against 2.5x in 2021), cost-out is a downside defence and no financial leverage is in use; from 2028 EBITA grows about 1.1x revenue and EPS about 1.1x, below the median company's ratio of about two. The cash-funded deal flywheel and the unused balance sheet are real loops that lift it above the AQ Group and Bravida examples, but the structure today converts growth into proportionate rather than outsized profit, below the Economic strength group's 72, which rewards returns rather than gearing.

FY2025 adjusted EPS and the FY2026 EPS growth rate are on the like-for-like adjusted basis (the basis notes are in the end notes).

Inference.

  • Double-digit growth arrives from 2028, and half of it is bought. From the 2026 base, EPS compounds at about 10.6% a year to 2030: one slow year, then 12% to 14% a year. Deals not yet announced provide about half of revenue growth and about half of EPS growth from 2028.
  • Growth is better balanced than in the past; the margin is barely higher. Revenue grew about 10% a year from 2020 to 2025, while EPS was flat from 2022 to 2025. The forecast margin sits less than a point above the 2022 to 2025 range, and about a third of the rise in the EBITDA margin is accounting: owned property and leases move cost from operating expenses into depreciation.
  • 2027 is the soft year by construction. EBITA grows about 8%, but EPS grows only half as fast because 2026’s financial gains (about SEK 26m, mostly currency) do not recur.
  • Cash is the strongest line from 2027. Free cash flow roughly triples on the cash-flow-statement basis (and rises more on the model’s mechanics) as the property programme ends and working capital stops absorbing cash. The rise in free cash flow is the most mechanical positive in the forecast: its direction is close to certain; the quarter in which it shows is not.
  • The balance sheet stays net cash. Free cash flow covers both the dividend and the deals. The company had net cash of SEK 178m at 30 September 2026; the model’s own net debt line is an artefact of incomplete source data and should not be used.

So what. The forecasts ask for less than OEM has already shown on organic growth, margin and cash, and for one thing OEM has shown for only a single year: the deal cadence. The forecasts need no real pricing power, no cost programme, no margin convergence with peers and no leverage.

Inputs I tested and left unchanged. (1) Organic growth in the second half of 2027: I considered raising it on October’s PMI, and decided that the model’s underlying 5% excluding the Irish order is the right central case. (2) The 2028 margin, which recovers by about half a point: this assumes the 2027 give-back reverses; I find it slightly generous and within the noise. (3) The 2026 dividend of SEK 1.90 against consensus of SEK 1.82: a judgement on the payout that I have no evidence to improve.

Counter-case. An earlier round of this analysis leaned its own 2028 to 2030 margin slightly down, citing five years at 15% to 16%, a growing central cost and acquired companies at about 14% margins. If the EBITA margin stays at 16.0% rather than rising to 16.7%, 2030 EPS is about 4% lower. Against that, the acquisition engine has more capacity than the model uses.

What would change my view. Down: fourth-quarter 2026 operating cash flow below SEK 250m, or no new deal announced by the first-quarter 2027 report. Up, for reported EPS only: amortisation below about SEK 28m in the fourth quarter, which would mean OEM has lengthened its write-off lives.

Against the market. Like for like, the model is in line with brokers for 2026; for 2027 it is 3% to 6% below the adjusted-basis brokers and 5% to 10% below the reported-basis brokers; for 2028 it is above consensus on revenue (+4.6%) and EBITDA (+3.2%). The model summary’s “+0.6% against consensus” for 2027 EPS compares an adjusted figure with a blended median and overstates the agreement.

Conclusion: The forecasts show a soft 2027 followed by revenue growth of about 11% and EPS growth of about 12% a year on a margin barely above the past; free cash flow is the strongest line, and unsigned acquisitions are the least proven one.

Score: 76, set by the Rater. About 10.6% sits just inside the 10-15% B band, so I place it at the bottom: FY2027 is a +4% digestion year, the margin path is less than a point above the 2022-25 range with a third of the EBITDA margin rise being accounting, about half of the growth from 2028 comes from deals not yet signed, and on the reported basis the rate falls below 10%.

Upgrades, 6 to 12 months

#7 Scope for upgrades to guidance, estimates and the narrative over 6 to 12 months

Evidence. The model sits below the brokers for 2027 and above them for 2028 (#6). Brokers assume about 6% organic growth and margin expansion in 2027. Two of FactSet’s four EPS contributors are on a reported basis, and at least one of them appears not to carry the amortisation of the 2026 deals; Redeye, which does carry it, cut its 2027 EPS by about 5% on 30 October. No broker models unannounced deals, and no broker has dated a capital framework.

Inference: the expected path of estimates, report by report.

I share an earlier round’s estimate that the chance of 2027 adjusted EPS reaching DNB Carnegie’s SEK 6.39 is about one in four.

On guidance, the only possible raise is a capital framework. On the narrative, the next step up is from “EQT may add leverage” to “OEM compounds at 12% to 15% with no dependence on the equity market”, but the step down to “organic growth has rolled over” comes first.

So what. The scope for upgrades is good over the next six months and poor over months 6 to 12. Months 6 to 12 are the weakest part of the case, and they fall inside Richard’s horizon. Over months 12 to 24 the scope improves again mechanically, because each deal is an upgrade by construction (about SEK 0.06 of EPS for every SEK 70m of acquired sales) and because a framework becomes more likely with every quarter.

Counter-case. The cycle extends, organic growth in the second half of 2027 is 5% or more, the gross margin holds and upgrades continue through the year: this is the bull case, which an earlier round of this analysis put at about 25%. Separately, a faster deal cadence in the first half of 2027 could lift 2028 estimates early enough to mask the cuts to organic growth.

What would change my view. Brokers cutting their 2027 organic growth assumptions before the reports, which would lower the bar to the model; a framework at the annual general meeting; or order growth holding in the July report.

Against the market. After a twelve-month run of upgrades, the market expects more of the same. I expect upgrades, then cuts, then upgrades of a different and more durable kind. The market and I agree on the direction of 2028 and beyond. The practical difference is timing: I expect the best moment in the stock’s revisions profile to come after the October 2027 report, not before it.

Conclusion: The scope for upgrades is positive to April 2027, negative across the middle of 2027 and positive again from late 2027, so over the 6-to-12-month window on its own it is below average.

Score: 36, set by the Rater. The 6-12 month window (May to November 2027) is the memo's weakest: guidance has nothing to raise except a capital framework (about 40% likely by end-2027, less inside the window), FY2027 consensus EPS is expected to fall 3-6% as brokers' 6% organic growth and margin expansion meet the Irish non-repeat and a +23% order comparison (about -0.45 times the 10% revenue growth rate, roughly the 25th-30th percentile), FY2028 EPS is about flat, and the narrative steps down to 'organic growth has rolled over' before it steps up. Below the fourth-set group's 50, which took in the April upgrades and the later deal-driven upgrades outside the window; the framework option keeps it above TT Electronics, close to IMCD.

Conclusion: Momentum in OEM’s estimates is strong, momentum in its share price is positive but stalling, peers’ estimates are rising too, and the price action since October says the market has begun to discount the good news.

Risk and simplicity

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts and expectations

Simplicity. OEM’s case is simple to state and to audit. Each quarter, three series tell most of the story: deals announced, cost of goods as a share of sales, and operating cash flow. Below EBITA the arithmetic is almost mechanical.

SEK 10m EBITA = SEK 0.057 EPSno debt, no hedging and a flat share count, so EBITA converts to EPS at a fixed rate

The range of plausible EPS outcomes (the cone). For 2027, EPS after minorities should fall between about SEK 5.45 and SEK 6.45, around a central SEK 6.03: plus or minus 8%, which is narrow for a cyclical distributor. The 2028 range widens and skews up (about SEK 5.05 to SEK 7.60, around SEK 6.84), because the leverage option adds more than an industrial relapse removes. Against consensus, the 2027 range is skewed down and the 2028 range is skewed up.

The five judgements that move the shares, with the arithmetic. Judgements 1 and 2 set the 2027 EPS range; judgements 3 and 4 set the 2028 to 2029 range; judgement 5, the group multiple, can outweigh any one of the others.

  1. Organic growth in the second half of 2027. One point of 2027 organic growth is 1% of SEK 6,258m, or SEK 63m of revenue; at a 27% drop-through that is SEK 17m of EBITA (1.6%) and, after tax and per share, SEK 0.10 of EPS (1.6%). A plausible error is two points on the year either way, which carries into the 2028 base. Two points up is the brokers’ view; two points down means a negative second half.
  2. The gross margin. Half a point on SEK 6,859m of revenue is SEK 34m of EBITA. The model already takes 0.2 points off the 2027 margin. Half a point of gross margin is worth as much as two points of organic growth, and the gross margin moves with the krona and with the lag in passing on costs.
  3. The deal cadence under a new chief executive. The model buys SEK 400m of annual sales in 2027, SEK 450m in 2028 and SEK 500m in 2029, at about 14% EBITA margins. With no new deals, 2028 loses about SEK 635m of revenue and SEK 89m of EBITA, gains about SEK 14m of interest on unspent cash, and EPS is SEK 0.43 (6%) lower; 2029 loses about SEK 1,150m of revenue and SEK 161m of EBITA, gains about SEK 25m of interest, and EPS is SEK 0.77 (10%) lower. The plausible error is half of that (three to four deals a year): 3% off 2028 EPS and 5% off 2029 EPS. For the return, two-year-forward EPS at March 2028 would be about SEK 7.65 at half cadence and about SEK 7.2 with no deals, against the model’s SEK 8.1. At the working fair multiple (#11), the 18-month return then falls from about 13% to about 6% to 7% at half cadence, and to about zero with no deals. In the no-deal case, about SEK 4 a share of idle cash would have built up by March 2028.
  4. The balance sheet. SEK 1bn deployed at 7x EBITA buys SEK 143m of EBITA; interest at about 4.25% costs SEK 42m; the pre-tax gain of SEK 101m is SEK 80m after tax, or SEK 0.57 of EPS (about 8% of 2028 EPS). SEK 2bn adds about SEK 1.15 (15% of 2029 EPS) and would take net debt to roughly 1x EBITDA, at or below the low end of peers (1.4x to 2.4x). If OEM paid 8x EBITA, the gain would fall to SEK 0.47 per SEK 1bn. If no framework comes, nothing is lost against the base case, so this judgement is one-sided.
  5. The group multiple. At March 2028, one turn of the two-year-forward multiple is SEK 8.1 a share, or 4.7% of today’s price. The multiple does not change EPS; it changes everything else about the return.

Risks by type.

Sudden and fundamental (low to medium probability). An industrial relapse (organic growth of −5% to −10%; EBITA down 15% to 25% in the first year before cost action; margin near 14%); a krona spike (a 5% to 10% EBITA hit for one to two quarters); a large mispriced deal under the widened mandate. None of these risks is existential.
Sudden and perceptual (the larger set). A discount-rate shock to all compounders (15% to 30%); a disappointing appointment; a third weak cash quarter that lets the market call 2026 a false friend; an accident at a peer; the arithmetic deceleration read as a cyclical turn. Thin liquidity (about USD 3m a day) amplifies each of these risks.
Slow. The sponsor’s eventual exit (EQT left Beijer Ref after about six years, so an exit around 2030 would be typical), rising entry prices for acquisitions, and digital price transparency.

Precedents. OEM’s own cycle record is reassuring on fundamentals: in 2001 to 2004 sales fell about 30%, and the company cut nearly a third of its staff and stayed cash-positive; in 2009 sales fell about 20%, with positive cash flow in every quarter. The sector’s record is not reassuring on valuation: in 2022 the compounders’ median multiple halved. Earlier rounds of this analysis put a realistic trough share price at about SEK 115 to 130 (a group multiple near 20x, with earnings intact or cut by up to 10%) and a 2022-style tail at SEK 88 to 100.

Trackability. OEM’s forecasts are easy to verify and hard to anticipate. OEM reports orders, backlog, the organic and acquired split, segment margins, cost of goods and cash every quarter. It discloses no price-volume split, no project terms, no deal multiples and no intentions. One measured input is missing from the files: the co-movement table for this stock is empty, so my estimate that about two-thirds of the share price’s variance is shared with the Swedish compounder group is a hypothesis.

Against the market. The market’s main stated risks are the multiple, the culture and the overhang from EQT’s eventual exit, and I agree with all three. The market under-weights two risks (the depth of the second-half 2027 slowdown and the lag in the gross margin) and over-weights one (that a de-rating could stall the acquisition engine).

Conclusion: OEM’s forecasts are simple, well bounded and easy to track, and their fundamental risks are moderate and survivable, while the share price carries larger risks from the group multiple, the succession and the optics of 2027.

Score: 61, set by the Rater. The earnings case is simple and trackable (deals, cost of goods, operating cash flow; no debt, flat share count, mechanical below EBITA) with a FY2027 EPS cone of about plus or minus 8% and fundamental risks that are moderate and survivable (relapse probability 15-20% with margin near 14% and cash released), but the share price carries larger flow-driven risks: a group multiple at the mercy of yields (15-30% shocks, halved in 2022), a dated succession binary, thin liquidity and a sponsor overhang. Between the two Risks groups (54 and 62), narrower than Bravida's cone and Indutrade's, just above Shell's resilience and below Kerry's gradual-erosion profile.

Lifecycle

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle

Evidence. The Master Dashboard’s rule places OEM in the Reinforcing phase. The supporting signs are plain: record orders, a twelve-month run of upgrades, a new acquisition engine with a year of delivery, and a share price above a rising long-term average. So are the signs of lateness: a fall on a beat, the first Hold rating, a valuation that has lost its company-specific premium, and a deceleration that can be dated.

Inference. I agree with Reinforcing, and would add “late in its first leg”. Since EQT’s entry the stock has passed through turning up and thesis broadening (figure above). Two more reports should reinforce the phase; then comes a stall test in the second half of 2027 that OEM’s fundamentals should pass and its optics may not.

What follows the stall test is the interesting part. If the acquisition engine has kept running and a framework has arrived, the stock enters a second broadening leg on a new thesis: a self-funded compounder choosing to use leverage. If the successor has slowed the engine and no framework has come, the stall becomes real. The odds favour the second leg, for three reasons: the precedents for succession are benign, the owner’s incentives point one way, and the engine needs no outside funding.

So what. Phase and timing argue against paying up now for peak-delivery characteristics, and for watching for the moment the market mistakes arithmetic for a cyclical turn. A collapse is unlikely for this business, because it has net cash, a protected margin and cash flow that rises in a downturn.

Counter-case. The first leg may have more room. With the cycle young and PMIs rising, the Reinforcing phase could last through 2027, and the stall test may pass unnoticed.

What would change my view. Year-on-year order declines before mid-2027 would bring the stall test forward. A framework in spring 2027 would start the second leg before the test arrives.

Against the market. Sell-side ratings (three Buys of four) treat the stock as in the middle of its Reinforcing phase, with a rising target price. The price action says investors are closer to my view than the brokers are.

Conclusion: OEM is in the Reinforcing phase, late in its first leg, with a datable stall test in the second half of 2027 and a credible second leg beyond it.

Score: 53, set by the Rater. I agree with the computed and memo Reinforcing, late in the first leg: record orders, a twelve-month run of upgrades and a price above a rising 200-day average, against a fall on a beat, the first Hold, a premium lost and a dated deceleration in H2 2027 that the market may read as a turn. The good news is largely known and a stall test comes first, with a credible second leg (framework, continued deals) beyond it, so it sits a little above BP's late Reinforcing and below Greggs's early turn.

The fair multiple

#11 The fair multiple

The working fair multiple is about 23.3x two-year-forward earnings. No guideline fair multiple is set for OEM, because the stock has under 24 months of multiple history. The model summary prints the guideline as 0.00x, but the model’s return arithmetic embeds one: today’s two-year-forward multiple is 25.4x on the model’s EPS and the multiple leg of the return is −8.1%, so the model uses about 23.3x at both horizons. I treat 23.3x as the working fair multiple and give my own view of it below.

Today’s multiple depends on the EPS basis, so three bases are shown. At SEK 171 the two-year-forward multiple is 25.4x on the model’s EPS, about 27.3x on the Master Dashboard’s consensus EPS (SEK 6.27) and 26.2x on FactSet’s series (23 October). The dashboard’s Phases page shows 28.9x, which equals the end-September price of SEK 181.4 over the same SEK 6.27, so it looks like a September-price reading. The model’s 8% de-rating would take the dashboard measure to about 25.0x.

Evidence.

  • Own history. The dashboard’s 18 months of history run from 23.4x to 29.9x, with a median of 26.6x. FactSet’s five-year series has a median of 26.7x and a low of 22.0x. An 8% de-rating puts the multiple 6% to 10% below its own median, in the lower part of its range.
  • Peers. The proven compounders trade on 22x to 28x current earnings; OEM is upper-middle on price-to-earnings and at the top of Redeye’s peer table on enterprise value to EBITA.
  • Growth and returns. Reinvesting about two-thirds of earnings at 12% to 15% on top of 5% organic growth produces earnings growth of 10% to 13% a year. That growth rate earns the proven-compounder median multiple, not a premium.
  • The group factor. Yields and Swedish small-cap flows mainly set OEM’s multiple, and that environment is currently hostile.

My view: a central fair multiple of about 24x, in a range of 22x to 26x. The guideline principle is a multiple high in the range for a stock in peak delivery and lower for one that is stalling. For a stock in the Reinforcing phase, 23.3x looks low at first sight. I think it is about right, and slightly prudent, for a specific reason: the 18-month measuring point (31 March 2028) falls just after the quarters in which the deceleration is fully visible, when the stock is most likely to be priced as stalling. My central 24x on the model’s EPS is 0.7 of a turn above the working figure, worth about three points of 18-month return. I would use the upper end of the range only once a framework is announced and the deal cadence has survived the succession; I would use the lower end if yields rise further or the appointment disappoints.

Counter-case. Higher: the owner will work for a premium multiple before it sells, broker coverage and foreign ownership (about 15%, against about 34% at peers) should widen, and a cash-funded acquisition engine deserves more than a geared one. Lower: the stock has no dividend floor (a yield of about 1%), carries a sponsor overhang, and Redeye, the broker that models the amortisation most fully, has a fair value of SEK 165.

What would change my view. A sustained move in the group’s multiple, in either direction, would move my range with it, because my fair multiple is a relative call inside a group that sets the level.

Against the market. The mean broker target price (#8) implies that the multiple holds near today’s level on rising earnings. I expect a modest de-rating, and so does the model. I agree with DNB Carnegie that OEM deserves proven-compounder treatment; I disagree that the market will grant it in full through the 2027 optics.

Conclusion: A fair multiple of about 23x to 24x two-year-forward earnings, a little below today’s and in the lower-middle of the stock’s short history, is right for where the stock will be in March 2028; the group, rather than the company, will decide whether that multiple proves harsh or kind.

Score: 55, set by the Rater. Neutral on both gives C; I place it in the lower half of the band because the multiple (about 25-27x two-year-forward) sits above the memo's working fair 23.3x and central 24x, and a modest de-rating is deserved for a stock moving into a visible deceleration, past its peak rate of change, with the group multiple hostile.

Total shareholder return

#12 Total shareholder return

The return of record (the Financial Analyst’s model, at the working fair multiple).

The horizons are about 17 and 35 months from today. The multiple and earnings legs multiply; dividends add. Value per share includes dividends received.

What drives the return.

  • Earnings: about 13% a year. The earnings leg is measured on two-year-forward EPS, which rolls from about SEK 6.7 today to about SEK 8.1 at March 2028. The earnings leg therefore looks straight past the soft 2027 and counts the 12% to 14% growth years. The soft year reaches the return only through the multiple, or through a lower EPS base if the second half of 2027 is worse than modelled.
  • What is inside the earnings leg. Roughly half of the earnings growth rate is organic growth and the slow margin rise, roughly half is unsigned acquisitions, and none is leverage. Because today’s two-year-forward EPS already contains some of those deals, removing them takes away about two-thirds of the 18-month earnings leg (#9).
  • The multiple: a single toll of 8%. The de-rating costs about 5.5 points a year over 18 months and under 3 points a year over three years, which is why the longer horizon annualises higher.
  • Dividends: a little over 1% a year, and falling as a share of earnings as cash goes to deals.

Put simply: the holder is paid the business’s compounding rate, less a one-off toll on the multiple, plus a small dividend.

How the 18-month return moves across cases (my arithmetic on the model’s figures).

So what. On the base case the return is respectable and unremarkable, and there is no valuation cushion: the dashboard’s valuation rating is D. The spread of 18-month outcomes is roughly symmetric around the base, wider than the EPS range, and dominated by two things that have little to do with 2027 earnings: the multiple and the deals. Over three years the skew turns positive, because the acquisition engine’s contribution accumulates, the leverage option has more time to be exercised, and the multiple toll is paid only once.

Counter-case. The return could beat the model on both the earnings and the multiple legs at once if the framework lands at the 2027 annual general meeting. The return could fall short with no fundamental failure at all if yields take the whole compounder group down.

What would change my view. The return is most sensitive to the entry multiple. Each turn lower at entry adds four to five points to the 18-month return, and a 10% lower entry price with estimates intact lifts the three-year return from about 34% to about 49%.

Against the market. Broker targets imply a return of about +18% over twelve months, which requires the multiple to hold and 2027 estimates to be met. The model’s return is lower because it assumes neither. Redeye’s fair value implies about −4%. The model sits between the two, and I think it is nearer to right than either.

Conclusion: At the working fair multiple the return is about 9% a year to March 2028 and about 11% a year to September 2029, earned almost entirely from earnings growth of about 13% a year, half of which depends on deals not yet signed, less an 8% de-rating.

Score: 58, set by the Rater. About 13-14% sits in the C band and maps to about 57-60, earned from about 13% a year of earnings growth (half from unsigned deals) less an 8% de-rating plus a small dividend; the spread is roughly symmetric (framework +22% to +37% against a group trough about -3% and a relapse about -28%) and the three-year check is supportive, so I hold it near the scale point.

Conclusion

#13 Summary conclusion

OEM is the right kind of company undergoing the right kind of change. The foundations are robust: high returns, a margin that survives downturns, no customer or supplier concentration, no debt, and an industry that rewards a patient consolidator. The change is real: an owner with control has lit a second engine, the deals are closed and performing, and the funding comes from the company’s own cash flow, which no market setback can switch off. The most powerful part of the change, the use of the balance sheet, has not happened yet and probably will.

The difficulty is that the market already knows the good part of the story and has not yet met the awkward part. The good part is priced at the group multiple. The awkward part is a 2027 in which the growth rate falls by arithmetic, the margin dips, brokers cut their estimates, and a new chief executive is still unproven. None of these developments damages the business. All of them can damage the stock, in a group whose multiple is hostage to bond yields.

For an investor whose test is an unusually positive skew in outcomes and upgrades, OEM is close to qualifying and does not qualify today. OEM qualifies when one of two things is true: the owner has declared its capital framework, which converts a probable option into forecast earnings, or the market has marked the stock down for a slowdown that the model already expects. The framework could come as early as spring 2027; the mark-down is most likely around the third-quarter 2027 report. Until then, OEM is a good business compounding EPS at about 12% a year from 2028, with a small toll on the multiple, and the work is to watch four dated tests: the appointment, the February cash-flow figure, the annual general meeting and the October 2027 report.

Four developments would make me more positive sooner: an operationally credible successor, deals continuing through the handover, cash conversion recovering in the fourth quarter and a framework before the summer. Three would make me negative: departures among the subsidiary heads, a large deal at a high price, or a gross margin falling while the krona is stable.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 64, set by the Rater. The input forces are clearly positive (a cyclical upswing peaking in rate around now, 66, and a funded, working acquirer conversion with a probable leverage framework, 70), but they reach profits only at about the typical rate: EPS compounds about 10.6% a year (the Universe median is about 11%) through a +4% FY2027, on a margin barely above the past, with half the growth from unsigned deals, so a mild-to-clear net positive in the 60s rather than the memo's B-level strength.

Foundations' Robustness: 74, set by the Rater. Top-decile returns (ROIC 92nd percentile), net cash, a margin held at 15-16% and positive cash through three downturns, no concentration and a fragmented, rational industry make a stable, predictable franchise that Richard's stability test rewards (topic 3 at 67); held below the 75 band's middle by no pricing power, heavy working capital, sponsor-serving governance, an unnamed chief executive and a cyclical rather than conservative delivery record (topic 4 at 54).

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 68, set by the Rater. In substance the case fits a Serial Acquirer Mechanical EPS Upgrader well (six to eight deals a year funded from free cash flow, each an upgrade by construction, earn-outs ahead of plan, a probable leverage option), better than the memo's C, which also counted the FY2027 cut sequence that belongs to timing; it is held below 75 by two loose elements: the acquirer's record is one year long and the cadence must survive an unnamed new chief executive, with 2026's weak cash conversion a current blemish.

Case Riskiness: 55, set by the Rater. The operating case is simple, ungeared and narrow (topic 9 at 61), but the equity case is less predictable than its operating lines: a cyclical distributor on about 25x whose multiple follows yields and Swedish small-cap flows, a long-serving chief executive leaving with no successor named, a sponsor overhang, and no management of the sell-side bar ahead of likely FY2027 cuts, which together sit a little below Richard's Arteche 60.

End notes

  • Forecast basis. The forecasts are the Financial Analyst’s model (update 2, base case). Its EPS is adjusted (before amortisation of acquired intangibles) and before minority interests, which the model does not deduct; after minorities, EPS is SEK 0.06 to 0.13 lower each year. FY2025 adjusted EPS and the FY2026 growth rate in #6 are on the like-for-like adjusted basis: the model’s own +38% compares adjusted 2026 with reported 2025, and after minorities the like-for-like figure is +29%. The FY2025 EBITA margin is the company’s. Free cash flow on the cash-flow-statement basis is about SEK 80m to 130m a year higher than the model’s, because the model counts acquired companies’ working capital twice. I changed no forecast input; #6 lists the inputs I tested and why I left them.
  • Consensus. “Consensus” is thin and mixed. FactSet names three brokers for EPS, and its mean implies a fourth; two are on the adjusted basis and two sit lower. The memo compares like with like and says which basis is used. Consensus estimates are shown by named financial year throughout, never on a rolling basis.
  • Two source checks. The latest Earnings Review does cover the third quarter of 2026 (reported 15 October 2026); I confirmed this in the review itself. One AlphaSense report states that the Deputy CEO takes over as chief executive on 1 January 2027; no company announcement in the files supports that statement, so the memo treats the successor as unnamed.
  • Earlier rounds of analysis. References to “earlier rounds of this analysis” are to the earlier sets of questions on OEM that preceded this memo; their figures are cited where this memo relies on them.
  • Return horizons. The return horizons in #12 are the model’s fixed columns after the last reported period. The two-year-forward multiples in #11 come from the Master Dashboard’s Phases page, FactSet and the model; no guideline fair multiple is set because the stock has under 24 months of multiple history.
  • A request to the Financial Analyst. The model should show the guideline fair multiple it actually applies (the summary prints 0.00x, the arithmetic implies about 23.3x, and the Phases page says none is set), and should state today’s two-year-forward multiple on one named basis, since the model and the Phases page differ in both price date and EPS.
  • Sources of the visuals. Default charts and tables come from FactSet, the Master Dashboard and the one-page summary of the Financial Analyst’s model (update 2). Richard’s five financial tables (annual history, recent periods, FactSet consensus, broker detail, segments) are drawn from FactSet and the model; in them, small raised figures are the number of brokers behind each consensus figure. Charts drawn for this memo (revision path, revenue growth split, EPS bridge, return on equity, EPS range, multiples, return waterfall, return cases, free cash flow and the judgements sized on EPS) take every figure from the memo text; where a bar is a residual or a cross term, its note says so.
  • Not shown. The ten-year financials table, which repeats the figures in the trajectory chart and the annual history table; and a return at the guideline fair multiple, which the model does not set for this stock (it prints 0.00x).

How to read this page

Every rating of this stock on one page: the Rater's 1-100 number, its letter and the Rater's own reason (at most three sentences, taken from the ratings file; nothing newly written). The number is the company's approximate standing in the Universe of about 1,300 listed European companies (90 = better than about 9 in 10; 50 = typical). A letter follows its item's rule: rank among the stocks scored (A the top 10%; B+ and B the next 15%; C+, C and C- the next 25%; D the next 25%; F the bottom 25%); or Richard's cut-offs on the measure for the four numerical topics (forecast financials, current momentum, the fair multiple, total shareholder return). On the change-forces items the number carries a sign (50 = neither positive nor negative) and the letter is the rank, so read the two together. "9th of 30 stocks scored" is the stock's place on that item. A dashed badge is provisional (fewer than 30 stocks scored).
